extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers, and students seeking an encyclopedic overview of Purdue Pharma and its role in the opioid crisis
extracted.subtask_description: A comprehensive Wikipedia-style company article summarizing history, products, marketing, legal actions, and societal impact of a pharmaceutical firm (here: Purdue Pharma). Intended to inform general readers and researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of clinical evidence for FDA approval
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether long-term studies and assessment of addictive capabilities were conducted before marketing approval (the page notes OxyContin was approved 'even though no long-term studies and no assessment of its addictive capabilities had been conducted').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights that Purdue obtained FDA approval in 1995 without long-term addiction studies; it cites that approval to prescribe for 'moderate to severe pain' was granted and that ambiguous label text ('is believed to reduce the abuse liability') later became a key issue in lawsuits and the 2007 felony conviction for criminal misbranding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and clarity of product labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the product label and package insert accurately and unambiguously reflect risks (example: the FDA-approved label text 'Delayed absorption ... is believed to reduce the abuse liability' was ambiguous and litigated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguous or misleading label language can be central to misbranding charges; the page cites that ambiguous wording became a key issue in subsequent lawsuits and the company's 2007 felony conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness of marketing claims about addiction risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether marketing statements (to doctors, patients, or the public) correctly represent the addiction and abuse risk (the page describes Purdue training reps to say addiction risk was 'less than one percent').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training sales reps to convey low addiction risk and promoting OxyContin as having limited potential for addiction were central to accusations of deceptive marketing; misleading the public about addiction risk led to guilty pleas and large fines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of approved indications and promotional scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether promotion expands use beyond evidence-based or approved indications (page notes Purdue promoted OxyContin for 'non-malignant pain', greatly enlarging the market beyond cancer-related pain).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents a nearly tenfold increase in prescriptions after promotion for non–cancer-related pain; promotion beyond appropriate indications is presented as a major driver of widespread prescribing and consequent harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics of sales and speaker programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether industry practices (free trips to seminars, paid speaking engagements, speaker bureaus) create improper influence on prescribers (the page describes all-expenses-paid symposia and recruitment for Purdue's national speaker bureau).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes more than 5,000 physicians, pharmacists, and nurses attended such symposia; these practices are presented as inducements that encouraged prescribing and were ethically problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of targeted sales strategies and incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether sales strategy targeted high-prescribing physicians and used incentives that could turbocharge sales (McKinsey advised focusing on highest-prescribing doctors; consultants suggested per-overdose rebates to distributors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cites McKinsey's role in focusing visits on high-prescribers and controversial proposals (e.g., rebates for overdoses) as examples of tactics that prioritized sales over public health; such strategies were later the subject of settlements and criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring, surveillance, and corporate response to abuse signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the company adequately monitored signs of abuse/diversion and took effective steps (the article notes Purdue had surveillance like RADARS and internal memos mentioning 'street value', 'crush', or 'snort', but responses were inadequate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence cited includes internal memos and DEA findings that Purdue's 'aggressive methods' exacerbated abuse; cases allege Purdue failed to follow legal agreements to track suspicious ordering or to contact authorities despite knowing of diversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of efficacy/dosing claims (12-hour cycle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether dosing-duration claims match patient experience and evidence (Purdue claimed 12-hour relief, but many patients experienced effect for eight hours or less, contributing to misuse and withdrawal-driven overuse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article references investigations and expert commentary that the 12-hour claim was inaccurate in many patients and that insisting on 12-hour schedules pushed doctors to increase dose size rather than frequency, exacerbating addiction risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to amend labeling and prescribing guidance when evidence changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the company updated labels or clinical guidance when evidence (e.g., shorter effective duration, reports of abuse) indicated changes were needed (West Virginia judge noted Purdue could have tested safety/efficacy at eight hours and amended label but did not).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial findings and settlements cited on the page argue companies have a duty to act on safety/efficacy evidence; failure to do so was characterized as deceptive marketing in some suits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with distribution controls and reporting suspicious orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the manufacturer and distributors tracked excessive or suspicious pharmacy orders and reported diversion to regulators (the Everett, WA suit alleges Purdue did not intervene or contact the DEA despite noticing odd patterns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegations include failure to follow legal agreements to monitor and act on suspicious ordering; settlements and suits have centered on costs to cities and states arising from such failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate financial transparency and avoidance of fraudulent conveyance
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether transfers of company funds to owners/related parties during litigation/bankruptcy were transparent and lawful (page references accusations of wiring at least $1 billion overseas and audits showing $10.7 billion withdrawn).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States alleged fraudulent conveyance and sought to hold family members personally liable; transparency of transfers is presented as central to settlement negotiations and litigation over recoverable assets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of corporate restructuring and non-debtor releases under bankruptcy law
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a bankruptcy-driven settlement can legally shield non-debtors (such as family members) from civil liability — the Supreme Court ruled the proposed releases were illegal because the non-debtors had not filed for bankruptcy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article recounts court rulings (including Harrington v. Purdue Pharma L.P.) finding that the Bankruptcy Code does not permit granting liability relief to parties that did not file for bankruptcy, making such settlement terms legally contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal accountability for corporate conduct and executives
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether corporate conduct and individual executives' actions constitute criminal violations (Purdue and certain executives pleaded guilty to misbranding; DOJ charges included conspiracy to defraud and anti-kickback violations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes corporate guilty pleas, individual pleas/fines, and internal DOJ memoranda recommending felony charges for executives; it highlights the difference between corporate/individual accountability and what was ultimately prosecuted or settled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-benefit outcomes of settlements and reorganizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether settlement terms (amounts paid, creation of public-benefit entities, access to addiction treatments, use of funds for victims/state costs) meaningfully address harms caused (e.g., proposals to restructure Purdue as a public beneficiary trust/public benefit corporation and to devote profits to plaintiffs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article describes proposed and approved settlement terms ($8B, $6B), restructuring into a public benefit corporation, obligations to provide addiction-treatment drugs to the public cost-free, and debates about whether settlements sufficiently compensate victims or allow accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics of philanthropy tied to profits from harmful products
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether accepting/donating philanthropic funds from families or entities whose wealth derives from products that caused public harm constitutes 'reputation laundering' (page references institutions dropping the Sackler name and activism by P.A.I.N.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists at least 20 institutions that have dropped the Sackler name and notes criticism that Sackler philanthropy functioned as reputation laundering; this criterion is used by cultural institutions and activists to evaluate donor relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public health impact assessment of product reformulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether reformulations intended as 'abuse-deterrent' adequately consider population-level substitution effects (Purdue's 2009 reformulation into an abuse-deterrent formulation is linked to increases in heroin use among people who previously abused OxyContin).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cites studies and analyses suggesting that ADF formulation made certain abuse routes harder, which in turn led many users to switch to heroin; such unintended consequences are presented as important to evaluate when approving or promoting reformulations.
